events.text: There were eggs once that kings came out of. Six in a gold box let down on Gujibong. One by the well at Najeong, with a white horse kneeling to it. One set adrift in a chest, because a king took fright. Nobody in the histories asks what laid them. You have sat a long time in the morning sun, and you have begun to ask. Kings seem to you a poor use of an egg. But a daughter's tree, in some farmyard, might do.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Go and look at a daughter's tree

effects.log: You come down the valleys slowly and speak to no one. Every farmyard with a girl in it has a paulownia at the corner. You find that you are counting them.

choices.text: No. You do not land where nothing is worthy. That is all you are

effects.log: You sing to the sun from the high ridge, as you always have. It is correct. It will go on being correct for a very long time.

events.text: The first tree is the best paulownia you have ever seen: pruned, fed, its trunk bound in silk against the frost. The house below has read the old books. They planted it to call you, and there is a dish of millet nailed up in the fork. That evening you watch the master of the house have a kitchen girl beaten for a chipped bowl. Afterwards he comes out, and bows to the tree.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Go. A good tree does not make a good house

effects.log: You are gone before the bow is done. He will tell them for years that you passed over, and they will believe him. You have learned what not to look at, at least.

choices.text: Stay the night. The tree did nothing wrong

effects.log: It is a very comfortable branch. You wake feeling that you have eaten something, though you never touched the dish, and all the next day you cannot find the note.

events.text: Market day. Old Gu's widow sells rice with a measure that has a false floor: you can see it from the roof of the salt shed, a thumb's depth. You note it. At dusk she carries a pot of that same rice up the hill to a neighbour dying alone, and spoons it into him, and stays the night. You wait for one of these to cancel the other. You wait most of the week.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Put her down as one woman, and keep looking at them

effects.log: It is an ugly piece of arithmetic and it will not come out. You stay the whole summer to watch it not come out. You have never stayed for anything.

choices.text: Strike off the valley. A false floor is a false floor

effects.log: You fly on. That is the last of that rice you will ever have to think about, you tell yourself, and you go on telling yourself as far as the river.

events.text: Someone is talking under the tree. She is five, and this is her tree, she says, planted the spring she was born. When she is grown they will cut it down and she will keep her clothes in it. She tells it this kindly. She also tells it that she took a persimmon, and who from. Then she looks up and sees you, all five colours and the long tail. "You are very big for a hen," she says, and goes in to dinner.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Stay, and hear the rest

effects.log: She comes back every evening with more. By the end of the month you know the whole village's business, as seen from about three feet up, and none of it is as bad as you thought.

choices.text: Leave before someone older sees you

effects.log: You are over the ridge by moonrise. You have been called many things by many courts. That one follows you a good way down the valley.

events.text: The carpenter has come for the tree. The girl it was planted for is to be married at the new moon, and the chest is owed. {npc}, who has kept this house since the fever took the others, stands at the foot with {his} hand on the trunk. {He} looks up. {He} is the only one who ever has. "The wood is not dry," {he} tells the carpenter. That is a lie, and a chest of pine will cost {him} a season's rice.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing, once, at the next dawn

effects.log: You have sung to the sun for centuries. This is the first time you have sung at a particular yard. {He} comes out with a bowl in {his} hand, and stands there until the rice burns.

choices.text: Go. That was a lie, and you heard it

effects.log: The tree stands uncut behind you, with nothing in it. You are a long way off before it comes to you that nobody has ever told a lie on your account before.

events.text: You sing at that yard every dawn now, and the whole lane is late to the fields. {npc} climbs the ladder, very badly, and sets a bowl in the fork: millet, the last good millet in the house, picked over by hand. A phoenix does not peck millet. It is in all the books. {He} has not read them. {He} sits on the rung and waits to see if you like it, with {his} own dinner going cold below.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Eat one grain

effects.log: It tastes of smoke and somebody's hands. It is the first thing you have eaten in your life that was not a principle. {He} nods, satisfied, and goes down.

choices.text: Leave it, and bring {him} a sprig of bamboo in seed from the south

effects.log: It is nine days there and back. {He} turns the thing over, eats a seed, and makes a face. Then {he} plants the rest by the well. It will flower in a hundred years, and {he} knows it.

events.text: Your mate comes down the valley and lands on the ridge above the house, and comes no closer. You fly up. For a long while the two of you look at it: the roof, the pig, the neighbour's fence, which has moved a hand's width since spring. Your mate turns that head a little to the left and looks at you, and you know every word of it. You have said it yourself, of better houses, to better kings.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Agree to watch one more year before you sing again

effects.log: So you sit on the ridge side by side and watch a house do nothing in particular. Your mate is quite content. Below you {npc} looks up each dawn, and goes in again.

choices.text: Go down and sing, with half a pair's voice

effects.log: You sing alone, which is not how it is written. It carries anyway. It is thin at the top, where the other part should be, and {npc} is the only person in the valley who says so.

events.text: At the new year {npc} walks four li to the sweet spring above the temple, carries back one gourd without spilling it, and climbs the ladder. "We cheat on the tax," {he} says. "My uncle drinks. The girl steals persimmons. I am telling you so that you know. Stay in this tree and sing, and nobody cuts it while I am alive. That is all we have." {He} pours the water into the hollow of the branch.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Drink. This is your perch, and you will say so every dawn

effects.log: You drink, and you turn to the east and sing it. No one in the lane knows that anything has been agreed. {He} climbs down with the empty gourd, misses the last rung, and laughs.

choices.text: Let it stand in the branch. A cheated tax is a cheated tax

effects.log: You fly at first light. The water stays in the hollow for some days, and then it is only a branch. {He} takes the ladder down, and uses it for the roof.

events.text: You cannot stop keeping the accounts. You know whose ox was borrowed and whose hen was found. Without quite meaning to, you have begun to go flat at dawn over any yard that has done something: half a tone, no more. The lane has noticed. "Bird was flat," they say at the well, and look at one another. Two fences have moved back. {npc} asks you, from the ladder, if you know what a terrible neighbour you are.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Go on singing the true account

effects.log: The lane becomes honest, in a sullen way, and stops asking each other in for a drink. They are very careful people now. You have done that, and you are not sure what it is.

choices.text: Sing it whole, over every yard, whatever they did

effects.log: It takes effort, and it sounds like nothing you were hatched for. The fences stay where they are. Somebody's uncle, coming home late, stands and hears all of it with the shoes in one hand.

events.text: A lean year for seed. No grove has flowered anywhere you can reach, and you have been getting light. {npc} has noticed. {He} is gone nineteen days. {He} comes back thin, and climbs the ladder with a pouch {he} paid too much for, from a peddler who swore by the southern groves. It is one part bamboo seed to three parts dyed millet. {He} does not know. {He} has sold the good pot.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Pick out the true seed, grain by grain, and leave the rest

effects.log: It takes all morning. {He} watches from the rung, sees what you are leaving, goes quiet, and goes down. The next week {he} walks back to find that peddler.

choices.text: Eat all of it, in front of {him}

effects.log: You are ill for two days, discreetly. {He} never learns anything, and {he} is very pleased about your feathers. You sing the next dawn a little hoarse, and very well.

events.text: The county magistrate has heard. A phoenix shows itself only under a virtuous ruler: that has been read, and it is wanted in the next report. The magistrate's clerk comes to the house with a good cloth and a better offer, and looks at the pig. The tree could be moved to the county office at no cost, and {npc} made keeper of it. {npc} says {he} will have to ask. The clerk laughs. {npc} comes out and looks up.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Fly over the county office at noon, once, and do not turn your head

effects.log: Half the town sees you go over. You do not slow down. The report goes to the capital anyway, with a different bird in it, and the clerk does not come to the house again.

choices.text: Stay in the tree, and sing as if no one had called

effects.log: The clerk comes back twice, less politely, and then there is a small matter of the tax for {npc} to settle. {He} settles it. {He} does not ask you to do anything about it, which you notice.

events.text: You come home late in the hungry month, and there is a lamp under your tree. {npc} and the uncle are digging. They put in four sacks of grain, the part the tax man will not find, and tread it down over the roots. {npc} looks up out of habit, and sees you. Nothing unworthy under the tree: that was the whole of what you asked. They will starve without it. {He} goes on holding the spade.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Come down and stand on the place, on the dirt, where {he} can see you

effects.log: You have never stood on a floor. You stand there till morning on the turned earth. {He} sits across from you and tells you all of it: who eats, and how much, and who will not. You understand it no better. But now it has been said.

choices.text: Look at the moon until they have gone

effects.log: They finish. In the morning you sing it whole. The house eats all that winter and lives, and that grain gives off a faint sourness in the branch, which only you can smell.

choices.text: Go. You said what you said

effects.log: You do not come back at the dawn, or the next. They eat the grain, and they live. The lane wakes up on its own at last, and is surprised by how dark it is.

events.text: {npc} has sworn falsely. A neighbour's boy took a sack from the county store, and the sentence is very long. {npc} stood up before the magistrate and swore the boy was under this tree with {him} all that night. Now {he} comes out at dawn, to the tree {he} named. On your breast is the pattern that means mercy, and on your belly the one that means trust, and until this morning they have always agreed.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing both, out loud, the mercy and the lie

effects.log: It is the hardest thing you have ever sung, and the ugliest. The whole lane comes out to hear it. {He} stands under it with {his} head up, and afterwards {he} asks if you are done, and goes for the ladder.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the boy live, and let the note go

effects.log: You sing it whole, and the boy comes home. Your belly itches in the rain for the rest of your life, in the place where the pattern is.

choices.text: Go. This was the last thing the tree could hold

effects.log: You do not stay for the morning. You go up to the ridge where the pair has always sung. Nobody there says a word about it, and that is the worst of it.

events.text: It is the pair's egg, by rights, and you carried it here without asking. You set it in the fork on a night with no wind. {npc} finds it at dawn: as big as a water gourd, and warm as new bread. Nobody has told {him} anything. {He} takes it inside {his} jacket, and sits up with it all that winter. In spring it cracks on the kitchen floor. What comes out is called {bk_child}. It is damp, outraged, and has ten toes.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing to it from the sill, where you have never come

effects.log: You land on a windowsill, on a house. It stops yelling, and looks for you with the wrong eye. There are five colours across its shoulders that week. {npc} keeps the pieces of the shell in the chest of pine.

choices.text: Stay up in the tree. It is out of your keeping now

effects.log: {npc} brings it out at noon and holds it up to the branch in both hands, as one shows a thing to a buyer. You look once, from a height. You sing no differently the next morning, and you have to work at that.

events.text: A second egg. This time your mate carries it down, at night, without a word, sets it in the fork, turns it a quarter as it should be turned, and looks in at the kitchen, at the smoke and the pig. Then your mate goes back up to the ridge. This is not approval. It is more like someone coming to inspect a debt. By spring there is {bk_child}, and {npc} has worked out how it is done, and sleeps.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Go up to the ridge, and sit with your mate

effects.log: Neither of you has anything to say. You sit there a whole season, side by side, and look down on that one small roof. Your mate has begun to look at it first thing in the morning, and denies it.

choices.text: Stay at the window, and learn to turn a baby

effects.log: It cannot be done with a beak. {npc} shows you the way of it anyway, on the sill, at some length, being tired. You have never been taught anything by anyone. You would not care to have that feeling twice.

events.text: {bk_child} is seven, and you have been watching from the branch for a sign since the shell. {bk_child} cheats at five-stones when the others look away, eats whatever is there, lies pleasantly to {bk_love} about the ink, and has never once looked up. There is not a mark on those shoulders. It is the happiest person you have ever seen. {bk_love} glances at the branch, and shrugs.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing to it as you would to anyone

effects.log: The lane gets its dawn. The child sleeps through it every time, mouth open. You go on singing at that shut door, with something that may be envy.

choices.text: Go flat over the yard, for the matter of the ink

effects.log: You go half a tone flat. {bk_child} does not even notice. {bk_love} does, and looks up at you for a long moment, and you correct it before the second phrase.

events.text: A feast at the headman's, in clean jackets. {bk_child}, seven and hungry, will not sit. All through it the child stands in the doorway with an empty bowl and looks at the headman's hands. Nobody has told {bk_child} about the boundary stone. Only you saw that. {bk_love} carries the child home. "The rice was wrong," says {bk_child}. At dawn a small voice on the top rung goes half a tone flat, over the headman's roof.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing with it, once. Then let {bk_love} see its shoulders in the sun

effects.log: Five colours, seven years after they faded. {bk_love} puts a jacket over them, and holds on for a while. That child will never once eat in peace. You have done that, and you are so proud that you cannot finish the phrase.

choices.text: Teach it the other note, the one for eating anyway

effects.log: You sing it whole over the headman, again and again, until a small voice gets it. It takes the summer. The child goes to the next feast, and sits, and eats, and looks across the lane at you. You know just what that rice tastes like.

events.text: {npc} cannot manage the ladder now. {He} has had a stool brought to the foot of the tree, and {he} sits on it at dawn in a blanket and has opinions about your upper register. "Forty years," {he} says, looking up. "The fences and the grain. You have been looking at us all that time. I would like to hear the verdict, if you have got it, before I go."
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Come down, and stand on {his} knee

effects.log: You have never landed on a person. You weigh much less than you look, and {he} says so. {He} looks you over from the beak down, like something paid for over a long time. "Well," {he} says, "you have got thin." You stay until {he} is cold.

choices.text: Give {him} the verdict, one fault a morning

effects.log: It takes the whole winter. {He} disputes most of them, and {he} is right about some. On the last morning you have run out, and {he} sends up a bowl of millet. You both know what that is, and it is not a bribe.

events.text: The stool is still at the foot of the tree. They have carried {bk_love} out to the burying ground at first light, on the shoulders of the lane, with those who cheated {bk_love} for forty years carrying a corner each. You are in the branch, with the best view in the county. Men plant a paulownia to call you, the old song says, and you do not come, and there is only the moon. Nobody ever says what happens if you do.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing, as on any morning

effects.log: You sing the whole of it, to the east, with nobody under it. It goes out across the valley. A long way off some person stops in a field, and looks up, and cannot think why.

choices.text: Do not sing. Not for a year

effects.log: The lane wakes late all that year, and the rice is late, and the headman complains. Then one by one, at dawn, they start taking their stools out to the yard to wait. You had not known.

events.text: Eighty years on, there are paulownias in five villages, one for every girl of that line, and they do not cut them without asking, though they could not say asking whom. They are known down the valley as the ones who send back the rice. They have been sued by everyone. They have never been rich. One of them, named for {bk_child}, is telling a rice dealer what is wrong with his scale.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing over that yard, whole and loud

effects.log: The dealer looks up. The namesake does not. It is a bad day for business, and it ends as their days end, with a lost customer and a very small dinner.

choices.text: Go half a tone flat over the scale, and see who hears

effects.log: Three of them look up at once, from three different yards, with the same expression. You have not seen that since you last looked in a spring. You go on with your morning, well pleased.

events.text: A clerk walks home up the valley with a bag and no post. There was a paper that wanted signing, and the clerk would not, and now there are no friends left in that office and no prospects in the county. {bk_child}'s people have come a long way to get here. The clerk stops under your tree for the shade, eats nothing, and looks critically at the branch. There are two small children at home who will want to know.
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Let yourself be seen, for as long as it takes to eat a rice cake

effects.log: The clerk looks at you, and does not bow. "You could have said something sooner," the clerk says, and gets up, and walks on, rather straighter. You suppose that is thanks.

choices.text: Stay hidden. It is a thing a person should do without a bird

effects.log: The clerk goes on up the road, having seen only a tree. That makes it worth more, by your reckoning. It is not your dinner they are short of, and you have never been sure of your reckoning.

events.text: You swore off houses, as you once swore off kings. {npc} has come to sit under your tree with a stolen jar, and is telling the tree, clearly and in order, everything {he} has done: the ferry fares, the short weight, the cousin. {He} is not sorry. {He} is just keeping the accounts, and nobody has ever kept them in front of you but you. "And you are up there looking at me," {he} adds, "so that is two of us."
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing the next dawn, in this yard, and let {him} know

effects.log: "You are flat," says {npc}, from the ground, without opening {his} eyes. You are. You have never been told so by someone with less right. You stay the winter, and then some.

choices.text: Go. You have done your reckoning once in this life

effects.log: You fly up before {he} has finished. {He} goes on without you. You can hear it from the ridge, and it is all quite accurate, and you keep listening until the wind changes.

events.text: A person walks up to your tree who ought not to know where it is. They take out a small bag of seed, and look at it, and look at you. They have eaten nothing on the road, it seems, because the inns were not up to much. They turn a long look on you from the beak down, the way you look at a house, and you feel it. "So you are the one to blame," they say. "You are smaller than I was told. Someone ought to say so."
events.arc: The Egg in the Daughter's Tree

choices.text: Sing them the whole of it, once, and let them judge

effects.log: They listen with their head a little on one side. "Flat in the third phrase," they say. You are delighted, and you have rarely felt so old. They leave the seed on the root, and it is very good seed.

choices.text: Look back at them, in the same way, until one of you stops

effects.log: It goes on until nightfall. Nobody wins. They get up, and bow about as far as you would have bowed yourself, not an inch more, and leave by the lower path without looking round.

events.text: You will not eat at your aunt's house. It is good food. You are six, you have been told about manners, and you stand in the door with the bowl held away from you, and you cannot say why. Later it comes out that the aunt has been selling the temple's rice. {npc}, an old friend of this house, walks you home in disgrace, sits you down, puts a boiled egg in front of you, and laughs until {he} has to hold the doorpost.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Ask what is funny

effects.log: "Nothing," says {npc}, wiping {his} eyes. "Eat your egg. It is only an egg." You have a feeling that it is not. You eat it, and you are sure about every bit of it.

choices.text: Go back the next day, and eat what is put in front of you

effects.log: It is delicious, and it sits in you like a stone. Your aunt pats your head. You have learned something very useful, and you feel as if you had swallowed a small cold coin.

events.text: Someone has broken the teacher's inkstone. You were not asked. You stand up and say who did it, which is your only friend, and then, since that was only half, you say that you were the one who dared your friend. The teacher looks tired. Your friend does not speak to you again. {npc} hears of it at the well, and finds you on the wall above the lane. "Was it true?" {he} asks. It was. "Did it help?" {he} asks.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Say that it was true, and that is the point

effects.log: {npc} sits with you until it gets dark, and does not argue. You have a clean feeling all through you, the whole of that winter, when you eat alone.

choices.text: Say no. Next time you will look out of the window

effects.log: You look out of a good many windows after that. There is a lot to see from them. Your friend comes back in the spring, and you have to sit on your hands.

events.text: One morning in your fourteenth year every bird in the valley is on your roof. Sparrows, magpies, a heron that has no business there, the whole ridge of the thatch sagging with them, all facing your door, and nobody making a sound. The lane comes out to look. The old people have a saying about when the birds do not scatter, and they do not say it in front of you. {npc} comes up with {his} tea, looks at it, and sighs.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Go out into the yard, and look up

effects.log: You look at them. They look at you. You feel very foolish. You lift one hand, and they go up all at once and in good order, which takes the roof off the pigsty. You are sent an account for the pigsty.

choices.text: Throw things until they go

effects.log: You are a very bad shot. A magpie looks at you on its way, with what you take for disappointment. They stop coming, and the whole valley goes back to its own noise.

events.text: Your sixteenth spring. You take off your shirt at the stream and a child starts to scream, and it is only the morning sun: across your shoulders are bands of colour as bright as a court robe, and they last till noon. {npc} brings out a paulownia box, light as nothing. Inside are pieces of a shell as thick as a rice bowl. "Sit," {he} says. "Kings came out of these. Nobody in this house has ever said so."
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Hear all of it

effects.log: A tree, a ladder, a bird that would not land. {bk_line}, on a kitchen floor. And {bk_anc}, who sang at this house and found fault with it. It explains a great deal. "That is why nobody asks you to dinner," {npc} says.

choices.text: Shut the box. You have fields to see to

effects.log: {npc} carries it away again. The colours are gone by afternoon. You keep your shirt on at the stream, and you find that you have stopped looking at anything very closely.

events.text: Word has got about that you cannot lie. It is not a compliment. Two brothers have walked in from the next village to ask you whose ox it is. They will take your word. So will their wives, and so, it seems, will the man who lent them the money. You have looked at the ox, and it is perfectly clear. {npc} watches from the step, eating a pear. "Do tell them," {he} says. "I have been looking forward to this."
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Tell them

effects.log: It is very quick. One brother has not spoken to the other since, you are invited to neither house, and by harvest they are bringing you other oxen from farther away.

choices.text: Say that you cannot be sure about oxen

effects.log: It is the first lie you have told anyone, and it takes you three tries. They go away puzzled. You go behind the shed and are sick, tidily, and {npc} brings you the rest of the pear.

events.text: A genealogist has come up from the county town with a fine brush and a case of old-looking paper. The man has heard there is something in your line about an egg. Very good. That is royal. For twenty taels the house can be written in under Bak Hyeokgeose, with dates. Half the great clans bought theirs the same way, and there are receipts. {npc} looks at you, looks at the sky, and goes to fetch something to sit on.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Throw the man out, with the paper

effects.log: The genealogist goes quite gracefully, and says from the road that it is a pity: it happens to be true, and that has never yet sold. You stand in the yard with a sheet of old-looking paper.

choices.text: Pay the genealogist, and read what is written

effects.log: It is a lovely piece of work, all of it lies, and one line of it true by accident. You keep it at the bottom of the box, and you do not sleep well for a season.

events.text: You were right about the grain ledger. You said so, at the district office, and the clerk who had been shaving it to feed a sick parent has been sent to the salt works for seven years. Everyone knows who said. Nobody blames you. They only stop talking when you come in. {npc} is shelling beans in the sun. "You were right," {he} says, not looking up. "How is that going?"
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Walk to the salt works, and take that household's winter rice with you

effects.log: It is six days. You do not ask forgiveness, because you were right, and you tell them that. They take the rice. You go each winter until the seven years are done, and nobody understands it, you included.

choices.text: Stay home. You were right

effects.log: You stay home. You are still right the next year, and the one after. It is very clean in there, and there is plenty of room.

events.text: {npc} has stopped asking what you think of the soup. {He} folds the cloths the way you fold them. You have never said a word, and you have checked the grain twice every night for years, and {he} has watched you do it. Tonight {he} is sitting on the edge of the mat with {his} back to you. "I would like to know," {he} says, "if I have ever once been good enough, or if it is simply how you look at everything."
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Tell {him} about the box, and the shell, and the bird that would not land

effects.log: {He} hears it to the end. "So it is not me," {he} says. It is not. It never was. In the morning you eat the soup, and you say that it wants salt, and {he} throws a spoon at you. That is the first good morning of your life.

choices.text: Say that the soup is fine

effects.log: It is a small lie, told gently, and you tell it every night after that. {He} knows just what it costs you. {He} goes on folding the cloths your way.

events.text: {npc} has put down {his} spoon. {He} looks at the bowl, and at you, and {his} face is one you know from inside. This morning you told the rice dealer that the sack was full weight. It was a little short. It was a very little, in a bad year. Nobody could possibly know. {npc} goes on looking at you across the table, small and polite and hungry, and does not pick up the spoon.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Go and take the dealer the difference, with {him} beside you

effects.log: It is a long walk for a handful of rice. The dealer thinks you have gone mad. On the road back you tell {him} about the shell, and what it will cost {him}. {He} eats like a wolf at dinner.

choices.text: Tell {him} to eat. Show {him} how it is done

effects.log: You pick up your own spoon and eat it all, looking at {him}. In the end {he} does the same. It is the worst thing you have ever taught anyone, and one day {he} may be able to sit at a table with someone. You hope so.

events.text: {npc} has come to the district to ask after you, and {he} says so to your face. {He} has a net over one shoulder, and {his} people have been at this trade since the hundred nets of Baekjangnyeong. {He} does not lie; {he} says it is bad for the work. The shell of a king's egg sells at court, and so does blood from what came out of it, to men with new family trees. A bowl would do. {He} would rather you agreed.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Settle it with your fists

ok.log: The net is very good, and you go through it. {He} gets up with a split lip, looks the tear over, and thanks you for your time. "You will hear from me," {he} says. It is the first thing anyone has said to you this year that you entirely believe.

fail.log: {He} has you on the ground in the time it takes to say so. {He} takes the bowl, and binds your arm properly afterwards. "That was fair," {he} says. It was. That is the annoying part.

choices.text: Say that you are nobody, and that it is a mistake

effects.log: You say it well, for you. {He} listens with great attention. "You went white," {he} says, "and you are holding your left hand. Nobody has ever been worse at this." {He} makes a note, and leaves you in peace for now.

events.text: {npc} once more, twelve years older, the net over the same shoulder. {He} settles by your fire. "It was easy," {he} says. "I only asked in each county who had been dismissed for refusing to sign. One lie, in any of those towns, and I would have lost you." {He} says it with respect. {He} has also found where {bk_anc} perches, and {he} would like you to walk {him} up there.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Finish it, here

ok.log: It does not take long. You fold the net and lay it on the fire, and it burns very cleanly. {He} was the only one who ever understood how you live, and you sit up with that until morning.

fail.log: {He} has read you for twelve years, and you have never once surprised {him}. You get away over the wall with two ribs gone. "I will still be here," {he} calls, and you know it is true.

choices.text: Look {him} in the eye, and lie. Say that you never heard of any of it

effects.log: It tastes like dyed millet. It is quite a good lie; you have been saving it all your life. {He} looks at you for a long while, knows, and starts to laugh. "Well," {he} says, "now I have lost you." {He} is gone by daybreak.

events.text: Food has gone flat. All of it, for a month now. You have lost weight, and {npc} has started watching you at meals. Then a peddler mentions that the bamboo is in flower in the far south: a whole mountainside, for the first time in ninety years, and the grove will die of it. Your mouth fills with water. You have never tasted bamboo seed in your life. You are halfway through packing before you notice.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Go. It is twenty days' walk

effects.log: You sit in the fallen seed on that dying hill and eat it raw, by the handful, with people from nowhere looking at you oddly. It is the best meal of your life. You walk home ashamed of how well you feel.

choices.text: Stay, and finish your dinner

effects.log: You finish it. It tastes of wet paper. You eat everything put in front of you that year, with good manners. Some time in the autumn the hunger stops. That is worse.

events.text: A new magistrate has come to the county. Everyone knows the magistrate is a thief, and your skin has started to itch. You wake before dawn on the roof, facing east, with your mouth open and no memory of the ladder. You know of a ridge with nothing on it. You also have a house, and debts. {npc} has come out in the yard with a lamp, and asks if you mean to come down.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Go up on the ridge till the magistrate is gone. You will not stand in that county

effects.log: Three years in a shed, on what you can carry. The magistrate never notices that you have left. But a few of the lane start sending up a sack, and one morning somebody is standing below your ridge, listening.

choices.text: Come down, and pay the tax, and say good morning

effects.log: You pay. You bow, at the proper height. You sit through the whole of the magistrate's banquet, and you eat, and you go home and wash your hands, and {npc} pretends not to see how many times.

events.text: {npc} takes you up at last to a bare slope that nobody farms. There is one paulownia on it, very old. You wait three dawns. On the fourth, something comes in out of the sun and settles, not on the branch you had been watching, and {bk_anc} looks at you. It looks at your hands. It looks at your shoes. It takes its time. So this is how it is. This is what it has been like for everyone who ever sat across from you.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Stand, and be looked at, all the way through

effects.log: It goes on until noon. There are several things it stops on, and you know them too. It goes away without a sound. {npc} asks how it was, and you ask if you may apologise to {him}, in general.

choices.text: Look back. You have a few remarks of your own

effects.log: You tell it about the egg, and the hard tables, and what it cost to be raised to this. It hears you out, with that head a little on one side. Then it sings, once, and you have to sit down on the ground.

events.text: You wake one morning knowing the day, and the slope. There is no bird on the slope this time. In the fork of the old tree there are things laid out, neat as an account: a wooden stool gone silver, a chipped bowl with one grain of millet, and a ladder rung worn through in the middle. You would never have thought it kept anything. {npc} reads the rung with {his} thumb, and says nothing, which is rare.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Take the rung

effects.log: It is only a stick. Someone climbed it, badly, for a very long time. You keep it over the door, and the next time you go to tell someone what is wrong with them you look at it first, some of the time.

choices.text: Take the grain of millet, and eat it

effects.log: It is very old, and it tastes of nothing, and smoke. You stand and chew. You would have sworn that a phoenix would not. {npc} looks at you, and starts down the hill, and you follow.

events.text: Your shoulders show the colours every morning now, and you have not sat through a meal without pain in years. "You cannot go on judging with half of you," says {npc}, "and eating with the other half." You could stay up here, and the feathers would come by autumn. You could go down and eat at the worst table in the county for a year, until it is only food. There is a third way, and {he} has never seen it done.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Go down, and eat what is put in front of you until it stops

effects.log: It takes a year, and you would not want it back. One morning the next autumn you eat a rice cake from a man you know to be a crook, and it is a very good rice cake.

choices.text: Stay up. Let the feathers come

effects.log: They come in by the first frost. The shirt goes first. In the lane they still bring a bowl to the foot of the tree, and you look at it from a long way up.

choices.text: Keep both: land where it is worthy, and come down to dinner anyway

effects.log: It should not work. You sit at table with all five colours showing, say just what is wrong with the soup, and have a second bowl. {npc} says that somebody climbed a ladder for this, a long time ago.

events.text: You told a neighbour today that the soup was the best you ever had. It was not. It came out of you as easy as breath, and you stopped in the lane with your mouth open. You walk round the village trying it out. You eat at the headman's. You eat at the inn. {npc} finds you behind the market with a greasy paper of fried dough, and the look of someone who has got out of prison.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Have another

effects.log: You have another, from the crook on the corner. Within five years you are a stout, pleasant, forgiving person. There are mornings you stand on the step facing east, for no reason, and go in.

choices.text: Go up once, with a bowl of millet, and leave it under the tree

effects.log: You do not look up. You leave the bowl and go. If anything up there has a remark to make about the millet, you are no longer in a position to hear it.

events.text: They plant a paulownia in the lane every time a girl is born, and they think you do not know what for. You sit up in the oldest one at dawn. Your feathers are correct. But you still have the taste of fried dough somewhere in you, and when the wind comes from the market you lose your place in the song. {npc} sets out a stool at the foot and shouts up the news, which you do not ask for.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Come down to one wedding a year, and sit in the highest tree in sight

effects.log: You come. You give no opinion at all, which they take as a blessing, and they are quite wrong. The bride looks up and laughs, and you find that you have no note for that.

choices.text: Stop listening to the news. Face east

effects.log: You face east. It is very clear up here. {npc} goes on shouting it up, for years, in case. You know who married whom, and you have not said that you are listening.

events.text: You keep feathers under your jacket and you have a seat at the table, and nobody knows what to do about you. You turn up at feasts in all five colours, eat two bowls, and tell the host what is owed and to whom. Then you go up to the ridge for the winter, and the lane gets on with it. {npc} says you are the most tiresome thing ever to happen to the county. There is a long line at your gate, with oxen.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Hear the oxen. Say the truth, and stay for dinner

effects.log: You tell them, one after another. Then you eat with both of them, which is the difficult part. The county has started to lie a little less, and to drink a little more with its neighbours.

choices.text: Go up for one more winter, and leave the gate shut

effects.log: They wait. You come back thin in the spring, with a bag of seed and a list of new complaints. Nobody has settled anything without you, and you are very sorry about how glad that makes you.

events.text: You have taken to counting, in your old age. Not their faults. Yours: the ones you got wrong. A fence that had not moved. A clerk who was only tired. You are sure of eleven, and you have them in order. You tell {npc} one evening, while {he} is mending a basket, and {he} says that you have left out the business with the pear tree. It had never occurred to you. That makes twelve. You are very pleased to have it.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Go and see the ones who are still alive

effects.log: You are carried to three of them. One does not remember it, one does and is rude, and one gives you lunch. You eat all of it and say that it is good, and you cannot for the life of you tell if it is.

choices.text: Write them down, and put the list in the box

effects.log: It goes in with the pieces of the shell. Someone in this house will open that box in a hundred years. They will be shocked, and they will check your figures.

events.text: A girl has been born in the lane, and they have brought the sapling round to you, as the oldest person going. It is a paulownia the length of your arm. They want you to hold it straight while they fill the hole. It will be grown in twenty years, and you will not. Your hands are not steady. Everybody stands about with the morning coming up red behind them. {npc} asks if it is straight enough.
events.arc: The Egg-Born

choices.text: Say that it is not, and make them do it again

effects.log: They do it again. They do it a third time. You are still not happy. They fill the hole in the end, around you, being polite. The tree comes up leaning a little to the left, and it is the best in the lane.

choices.text: Say that it is straight enough

effects.log: It is the first time in your life you have said so. They all look at you. You let go, and it stays up, and somebody brings you a stool, and you sit and watch it do nothing at all until the sun is well up.
